newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland blames chaos in Russia for ship's detention.
newsitem.headline: Poland blames chaos in Russia for ship's detention.

text.p: Poland's prime minister demanded on Tuesday that Moscow honour repeated promises to free a Polish trawler held by officials at sea off Kamchatka.

"We expect to be informed of the rapid release of our ship without any claims -- and such claims have not yet been made -- that it has broken any legal provisions," PAP news agency quoted Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz as telling reporters.
"In our view it has not infringed any," he added.
According to Polish accounts, Russian environment protection and border guard officials detained the Aquarius, with its 79 crew, on the Sea of Okhotsk on February 27.

The chief allegation was that it had begun fishing a day before its official permit allowed -- a charge disputed by the ship's owners, who have incurred heavy losses during the time the vessel has been prevented from fishing.

While top Russian officials have repeatedly agreed to free the ship, guards continue to occupy it, blocking radio links with owners or the crew's families and forcing it to head for port on the Kamchatka peninsula.
"The problem is there is no coordination between various authorities in Russia," a clearly exasperated Cimoszewicz complained earlier, in an interview with public radio.

"The Foreign Ministry and fisheries committee recognise the actions taken towards the Polish vessel are without basis, to be condemned, they apologise, they inform us they have issued orders to release the vessel -- and meanwhile someone on the spot takes completely different actions," Cimoszewicz said.

The latest assurance was made by Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Avdieyev, who informed Poland's ambassador in Moscow that fishery protection and border officials had been told to free the ship, which is now in the Kurile straits, the Polish Foreign Ministry said.
This followed a protest lodged on Monday by Poland's Interior Minister Leszek Miller, who was visiting Moscow, with his Russian counterpart Anatoly Kulikov.

"I understand it will be formally freed when it reaches the nearest port," Polish Foreign Ministry spokesman Pawel Dobrowolski said, adding that this would end the diplomatic issue although some financial matters might still need clearing up.
He told Reuters that Avdieyev had argued the ship had broken some rules, but had expressed regret for a lack of coordination on Russia's side.

Cimoszewicz said on the radio he hoped the ship's prolonged detention was just an incident without wider significance, adding: "I cannot imagine that in Moscow someone may be consciously trying to stir up this incident."
Moscow opposes former Soviet satellite Poland's bid to join NATO, and some Russian actions in recent years have been seen in Warsaw as an attempt to drive home these objections.
Although bilateral relations have improved in the past two years, especially economic ties, Poland's fishing on the Okhotsk Sea has sparked tough talk in the two capitals.
